md:
### Pulmonary metastasectomy at a glance

| Item | Point |
|---|---|
| Selection | Primary controlled; usually no extrathoracic metastases; adequate surgical candidate; complete resection anticipated |
| Strong prognostic factors (IRLM) | Disease-free interval, number of metastases, histology of the primary |
| Imaging | CT is the gold standard (CT and HRCT 100% sensitive for nodules of 10 mm or more); PET has low sensitivity under 10 mm and mainly excludes extrathoracic disease |
| Small nodules | A few nodules of several millimetres are usually watched; as they approach 1 cm, most are referred if isolated and the primary is controlled |
| Approach | Usually VATS or robotic. Open palpation finds more lesions in some series but has not improved survival. Bilateral disease: one operation or staged, by sternotomy or clamshell |
| Extent | Usually non-anatomical wedge; lobectomy for central lesions; pneumonectomy rarely |
| Nodes | Assess before and during surgery; involvement means poorer survival |
| Unfit or refusing surgery | SABR (small lesions; difficult with many) or radiofrequency ablation (small, away from the mediastinum); isolated lung perfusion is investigational |
| Outcome (IRLM) | 5-year survival 36% after complete resection against 13% after incomplete resection |

Source: summarised from "Pulmonary metastasectomy (TSRA ch. 15)" in this tab.
anchor: More than one metastasis does not consistently predict worse survival

md:
### Surgery for mycobacterial disease at a glance

| | Tuberculosis | Non-tuberculous mycobacteria |
|---|---|---|
| Resistance terms | Multidrug resistant: isoniazid and rifampicin. Extensively resistant: those two, a fluoroquinolone and an injectable agent | Not stated |
| When to operate | Localised resistant disease with adequate reserve and: sputum positive after 6 months of treatment; extensively resistant disease unlikely to be cured by drugs; or a complication (bronchopleural fistula, life-threatening haemoptysis) | Failure to convert at 6 months, macrolide resistance, or localised cavitary disease |
| Before the operation | Operate after culture conversion where possible | Raise albumin above 3 g/dL |
| At operation | Lobectomy gives better results than pneumonectomy | Dense adhesions and an extrapleural dissection; cover the stump |
| After | Complete the drug course | Fistula rates are high |

Source: summarised from "Tuberculosis and other mycobacteria" in this tab.

### Oesophagus: numbers at a glance

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Length | About 25 cm (men), 23 cm (women): cervical about 5 cm, thoracic about 20 cm, abdominal about 3 cm |
| Upper sphincter | 1 to 2 cm high-pressure zone; the narrowest point and commonest site of iatrogenic perforation; about 15 cm from the incisors |
| Lower sphincter | About 40 cm from the incisors; 2 to 3 cm long; resting pressure 14 to 34 mmHg; relaxes for about 5 seconds as the bolus enters the stomach |
| Narrowings | Upper sphincter; aorta and left main bronchus (average diameter 16 mm); hiatus |
| Muscle | Striated upper third, mixed middle third, smooth distal third |
| Vagi | Reform as left (anterior) and right (posterior) about 3 cm above the diaphragm |
| Primary peristalsis | 3 to 6 cm/s; lasts 10 to 15 s |
| Upper sphincter after a swallow | Pressure rises to twice resting, then settles |

Source: summarised from "Oesophageal anatomy and physiology (TSRA ch. 30)" in this tab; the 15 cm distance from "Oesophageal stenting (TSRA ch. 37)".
anchor: a single primary contraction lasts 8 to 10 s

md:
### Airway obstruction work-up at a glance

| Step | What it gives |
|---|---|
| History | Exertional dyspnoea progressing to rest, noisy breathing, wheeze or stridor; often mislabelled adult-onset asthma. Changed voice or stridor: glottic or subglottic disease. Hoarseness with a tumour: nerve or nodal involvement |
| CT with coronal and sagittal reconstructions | Where the lesion starts and ends and how much subglottic space remains; inspiratory and expiratory scans show malacia |
| Flexible bronchoscopy | Diameter, extent, distance from the cords, mucosal inflammation |
| Rigid bronchoscopy at the same sitting | Dilates or cores out and secures the distal airway; be ready for an emergency tracheostomy, because the scope can occlude a critical stenosis |
| Flow-volume loop | Shows fixed obstruction but adds little |
| Buying time | Steroids, nebulised adrenaline and heliox; benign obstruction is rarely a true emergency |

Source: summarised from "Stridor and airway obstruction: assessment" in this tab.
anchor: Benign obstruction is rarely a true emergency.
